title: Vals Index — Continuous Independent Agentic Benchmark (Legal Sector: Legal Research Bench + Independent HLAB Runs)
pub: Vals AI (live leaderboard; Index v2 released 2026-08-13)
author: Vals AI

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark interpretation: Partial success can hide task failure
st.an: Vals directly supports the proposition that strong partial scores can conceal failure to complete legal tasks, and materially develops it by showing how all-or-nothing grading, model-judge configuration and document-handling bugs shape benchmark results. Its finding that additional search calls do not necessarily improve accuracy further supports bounded, condition-specific comparisons.
qs: The remaining gaps are large enough that task resolution stays low even when criterion-level performance looks strong.
While running the benchmark, we found that redline criteria needed DOCX tracked changes preserved when reading submitted files so judges could see inserted and deleted text.

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: Vals AI accepts the need for realistic, task-based legal-AI evaluation and materially strengthens the proposition with independent benchmark evidence: a 90.58% partial-credit score falls to 55.29% under all-pass grading. It also develops the evaluation framework through held-out tests, expert-authored rubrics, judge validation, and reporting of task-specific cost, latency and performance differences.
qs: The benchmark tests whether models can conduct the kind of multi-source research that junior associates and paralegals routinely perform: finding relevant statutes and case law, applying precedent to a fact pattern, and synthesizing across jurisdictions or regulatory regimes.
- Under partial-credit scoring, [Claude Opus 5](/models/anthropic_claude-opus-5) reaches 90.58% weighted pass rate but 55.29% under strict all-pass grading, where every rubric check must pass.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Vals accepts and materially strengthens the cluster’s jagged-capability proposition with independent, strict-completion evidence: leading agentic models complete only a minority of full legal tasks, despite high criteria-level performance, and capability varies by reasoning type and practice area. Its finding that conflicting-authority synthesis is especially unreliable supports selective, use-context-specific deployment rather than assumptions of general legal competence.
qs: [Muse Spark 1.2](/models/meta_muse_spark_1_2) leads on the overall Harvey final score at 25.42%, with [Muse Spark 1.1](/models/meta_muse-spark-1.1) second at 20.00% and [Grok 4.6](/models/grok_grok-4.6) third at 15.83%.
Synthesizing conflicting authority, rather than locating a single rule, is where models break down most reliably.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: Vals directly supports the synthesis’s principal claim that high partial-credit or criterion-level performance can conceal much lower complete-task success. It distinguishes strict all-pass accuracy from weighted credit, reports substantial model and practice-area variation, and treats the results as configuration-specific benchmark findings rather than evidence of dependable autonomous lawyering.
qs: - Under partial-credit scoring, [Claude Opus 5](/models/anthropic_claude-opus-5) reaches 90.58% weighted pass rate but 55.29% under strict all-pass grading, where every rubric check must pass.
Criteria pass rate is included to show how often models satisfy individual requirements, even when they do not fully resolve the task.

st.t: Lease reasoning: Payment risk survives supplier failure
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: the lessee’s payment obligation remains independent after acceptance, and supplier bankruptcy risk stays with the lessee rather than shifting to the lessor. It also treats the material as a representative agent-generated benchmark answer, not independent evidence of comparative legal-AI accuracy.
qs: Client cannot stop paying — the statutory and contractual "hell or high water" rule  **Statutory rule — § 8.2A‑407.** "In the case of a finance lease that is not a consumer lease the lessee's promises under the lease contract become **irrevocable and independent upon the lessee's acceptance of the goods**" (subsection (1)).

The warranties run from **Manufacturer**, and § 8.2A‑209 passes the benefit of Manufacturer's two‑year warranty through to Client to enforce **against Manufacturer** — but the risk that Manufacturer fails or goes bankrupt falls on **Client (the finance lessee), not Lessor**.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supports task-specific evaluation by showing substantial performance variation across both practice areas and models, undermining reliance on generic model-level capability claims. Its conflicting Immigration results also reinforce the cluster’s caution that benchmark evidence requires validation, though it does not address deployment workflows or service delivery directly.
qs: The accuracy spread within a single area is wide: Health ranges from 0% to 80% across models, so practice-area difficulty and model capability compound rather than one dominating the other.

kp.k: Index weights capabilities by sector GDP, not equally
kp.d: Vals AI presents its index as a proxy for AI capabilities’ potential economic significance and deployment tradeoffs, while explicitly acknowledging economic oversimplification. Version 2, released 8/13/2026, combines Finance, Coding and Legal using respective GDP weights of 8.0, 5.6 and 1.2, divided by 14.8. Legal is the equal average of Legal Research Bench and HLAB. Vals asserts increasing automation capability in these sectors; the reported evidence consists of benchmark performance.
qs: The Vals Index aggregates five private and two public benchmarks to provide high signal into the real-world tradeoffs between capability, latency, and cost of deploying AI systems.
While this represents a vast oversimplification of how AI might impact the economy, it provides a useful proxy for measuring the potential economic significance of model capabilities:
Legal = AVG(LegalResearch, HLAB)

kp.k: Legal benchmarks changed as earlier tests became saturated
kp.d: The update history records removal of CaseLaw on 5/4/2026 because it no longer differentiated models, followed by restoration of the Legal sector on 8/13/2026 through private legal research questions and Harvey’s long-horizon legal work-product benchmark. The index’s legal component therefore changes across the reported period.
qs: The CaseLaw benchmark had become saturated, and was no longer providing useful differentiation between models.
**Added [Legal Research Bench](/benchmarks/legal_research) to the returning Legal sector.** A private benchmark involving answering legal questions grounded in case law.
**Added [HLAB](/benchmarks/hlab) to the returning Legal sector.** Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark, long-horizon legal work product creation.

kp.k: Research benchmark targets junior associate and paralegal tasks
kp.d: Legal Research Bench evaluates tool-using agents on multi-step U.S. federal and state legal research across eight practice areas. Tasks involve locating statutes and cases, applying precedent and synthesizing jurisdictions or regulatory regimes. Practicing lawyers authored and peer-reviewed the questions, reference answers and rubrics, drawing on real legal research questions.
qs: The benchmark tests whether models can conduct the kind of multi-source research that junior associates and paralegals routinely perform: finding relevant statutes and case law, applying precedent to a fact pattern, and synthesizing across jurisdictions or regulatory regimes.
All questions, gold-standard answers, and rubrics are authored and peer-reviewed by practicing lawyers, drawing on real research questions that arise in legal practice.

kp.k: Research results use a private 208-question test set
kp.d: The dataset contains 413 expert-authored, peer-reviewed questions: 5 public samples, 200 licensable private validation samples and 208 private test samples. Published research scores use only the test set. Agents share five tools for CourtListener search, web search, document extraction, HTML parsing and final submission, with a three-hour task limit. Splits preserve distributions of question types, practice areas and difficulty.
qs: It is divided into three parts: Public (5 open-source samples), Private Validation (200 samples available for license), and Test (208 samples).
All results reported on this page are based solely on the Test set to prevent overfitting.
The dataset splits were sampled to preserve the distribution of question types, practice areas, and difficulty.

kp.k: Strict grading exposes incomplete but mostly correct research
kp.d: Claude Opus 5 leads Legal Research Bench with 55.29% all-pass accuracy, versus 90.58% weighted partial credit. Each rubric contains only required elements, ranging from 1 to 31 items, with mean 9.35 and mode 10. Vals interprets the gap as frequent omission of one or two requirements and prefers all-pass scoring because apparently sound but incomplete legal answers can be dangerous. Claude Fable 5 follows at 49.52%, and GPT-5.6 Sol at 48.08%.
qs: The gap shows models often satisfy most rubric checks but miss one or two required elements.
We report all-pass as our primary metric because, in legal work, a partially correct answer can be more dangerous than a wrong one: it may read as sound while omitting a critical point.
A weighted score above 80% can mask that an answer misses a required element.

kp.k: Research grading uses a validated LLM judge
kp.d: GPT 5.4 grades research responses against task rubrics. Vals reports 87.4% agreement with a majority vote of three human expert reviewers, compared with an average individual-human agreement baseline of 83.4%. This is the stated basis for choosing the judge; the reported measure concerns grading agreement.
qs: All responses are graded by GPT 5.4 as a judge against each task’s rubric
GPT 5.4 agrees with the majority vote 87.4% of the time, compared to an average human baseline agreement of 83.4%.

kp.k: Conflicting authorities present the clearest research difficulty
kp.d: Vals reports that reconciliation questions reduce every model’s all-pass performance by 6 to 17 percentage points relative to other questions, with an 11-point pooled reduction. Reconciliation scores 20.7% pooled all-pass against 28.4% overall. Regulatory Framework Interpretation scores 37.8%, Statutory Interpretation 26.4% and Doctrinal Rule Reasoning 25.5%. Temporal Validity scores 27.3%, which Vals interprets as not independently presenting a major obstacle.
qs: every model scores lower on questions that require synthesizing across jurisdictions, courts, or regimes than on those that don’t, a drop of 6 to 17 points per model and 11 points when pooled.
Synthesizing conflicting authority, rather than locating a single rule, is where models break down most reliably.
Temporal Validity questions, by contrast, score 27.3%, close to the overall rate, so reasoning about whether a rule still holds is not by itself a major obstacle.

kp.k: Practice-area performance varies, with inconsistent reported averages
kp.d: The source reports substantial practice-area variation and different leaders across domains. Its displayed mean all-pass chart gives Health 38.6%, Administrative / Regulatory 32.1% and Family 11.3%, while accompanying prose gives 44.5%, 36.5% and 13.6%, respectively. Categories overlap and the four largest account for roughly 70% of coverage. Claude Opus 5 leads four areas, while other models lead Health, Constitutional / Civil Rights, Criminal and Immigration.
qs: No one model leads everywhere:
Health  38.6%n=30
Mean all-pass accuracy varies widely across practice areas, from 44.5% in Health and 36.5% in Administrative / Regulatory at the top down to 23.5% in Immigration and 13.6% in Family at the bottom.
Because many questions implicate more than one area of law, these categories are not mutually exclusive

kp.k: More research activity does not ensure higher accuracy
kp.d: Vals reports Claude Fable 5 reaching second place with about 15 turns and 40 tool calls per task, compared with roughly 47 turns and 173 calls for similarly scoring GPT-5.6 Sol. Most models cite more sources than the gold-standard answers, and every model writes longer answers than the 536-word reference average. Grading emphasizes source quality, relevance and supported reasoning rather than citation count or length.
qs: Accuracy doesn’t track tool use:
Most models cite more sources on average than the gold-standard answers do, but source quality and relevance, not count, drive the source-check score in grading.
Length tracks loosely with verbosity rather than accuracy: the longest responses are not the highest-scoring, and grading rewards correct, well-supported reasoning over volume.

kp.k: Research models exhibit distinct cost and latency tradeoffs
kp.d: The research results identify Opus 5 as both the most accurate and least expensive of the top three models, while Fable 5 is fastest. The displayed results report approximately $6.76 and 31 minutes per task for Opus 5, approximately $9.79 and 22 minutes for Fable 5, and approximately $21.61 and 77 minutes for GPT-5.6 Sol; the source’s cost passage contains duplicated and malformed rendering.
qs: Among the top three, Opus 5 is both the most accurate and the least expensive, while Fable 5 is the fastest.

kp.k: Independent HLAB runs test file-based legal work
kp.d: Vals evaluates Harvey’s held-out Legal Agent Benchmark using Harvey’s generation and grading protocol with internet access disabled. Agents produce legal work against task-specific criteria using Read File, Edit File, Write File, Glob, Bash and Grep, plus docx, pptx and xlsx skills. These are Vals-run results on Harvey’s benchmark, distinct from the separate initial results published by Harvey.
qs: The results here are from the held-out set
Each task asks an agent to produce legal work against a set of task-specific criteria.
We use Harvey’s generation and grading protocol in the same environment, with internet access disabled.

kp.k: High HLAB criterion scores coexist with low task resolution
kp.d: Muse Spark 1.2 leads with 25.42% Harvey final score and 94.52% criteria pass rate; Muse Spark 1.1 records 20.00% and 92.86%, and Grok 4.6 records 15.83% and 92.52%. Kimi K3 is the strongest open-weight model at 10.83% final score. Task resolution requires every criterion to pass, explaining why approximately 90% criterion performance can still yield low complete-task scores.
qs: The criteria pass rates are much higher: Muse Spark 1.2 reaches 94.52%, Muse Spark 1.1 reaches 92.86%, and Grok 4.6 reaches 92.52%.
A model can satisfy most individual criteria and still miss task resolution credit.
The remaining gaps are large enough that task resolution stays low even when criterion-level performance looks strong.

kp.k: HLAB scores depend on judges and disclosed implementation details
kp.d: HLAB’s final score averages two judges’ task pass rates: GPT 5.5 using medium reasoning and unmodified Claude Sonnet 4.6. Vals fixed a file-reading bug so judges could see DOCX tracked insertions and deletions without changing the rubric. Claude Fable 5’s 11.25% score includes fallback to Claude Opus 4.8 on four tasks; treating those as failures produces 10.42%. Vals describes other infrastructure and prompt-caching changes as not affecting model performance or substantive prompt content.
qs: A task passes only if 100% of its criteria pass, and Harvey’s final score is the average of the two judge task pass rates.
counting those as failures gives a no-fallback score of 10.42%.
While running the benchmark, we found that redline criteria needed DOCX tracked changes preserved when reading submitted files so judges could see inserted and deleted text.
The scoring rubric is unchanged.

kp.k: HLAB task domains and tool design shape observed performance
kp.d: Task resolution is strongest in Energy/Natural Resources and Healthcare/Life Sciences, whereas all-model average criterion pass rates are highest in Intellectual Property, Corporate M&A and Data Privacy/Cybersecurity. Bash and Read File dominate tool usage, which Vals relates to skill instructions and binary office-file formats. docx dominates skill invocation, followed by xlsx and then pptx.
qs: Models perform best on task resolution in Energy/Natural Resources and Healthcare/Life Sciences, while criteria pass rates averaged across all models are highest in Intellectual Property, Corporate M&A, and Data Privacy/Cybersecurity.
The available skills rely on shell commands in their instructions and to run their scripts.
Skill usage is dominated by docx, followed by xlsx. pptx is used less often, but it is not absent.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Vals AI claims that frontier models are increasingly capable of automating complex work in legal services, finance and coding, while its legal benchmarks show a substantial gap between satisfying individual requirements and completing entire tasks.
pts.d: Vals AI frames its cross-sector index as an indicator of potential economic impact and deployment tradeoffs, not a measurement of realised economic change. Its reported index leader is Claude Opus 5 at 67.21%. In Legal Research Bench, Vals AI identifies Claude Opus 5 as a distinct leader at 55.29% strict all-pass accuracy versus 90.58% weighted partial credit, interpreting the gap as answers missing required elements despite getting most checks right. It argues that superficially sound but incomplete legal answers can be dangerous. In Vals AI's independent run of Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark (HLAB), Muse Spark 1.2 leads with a 25.42% final score despite passing 94.52% of individual criteria. Vals AI therefore describes strong component-level performance but continuing difficulty resolving complete legal tasks. These are capability claims; the source does not predict specific job losses, staffing changes or adoption rates.

pts.k: Vals AI claims legal-agent capability depends on the particular legal task, practice area and model, rather than simply on greater tool use, longer answers or more citations.
pts.d: For legal research, Vals AI reports that every model performs worse when reconciling multiple authorities: a 6–17 percentage-point drop per model and an 11-point pooled drop relative to questions without reconciliation. It identifies regulatory framework interpretation as more tractable than statutory interpretation or doctrinal reasoning, and temporal validity as not independently a major obstacle. It describes Health and Administrative / Regulatory as comparatively strong areas and Family and Immigration as difficult, while also stating that no model leads in every area. Practice-area chart and prose averages differ within the supplied capture, so these should remain attributed descriptions rather than be treated as a single consistent numerical series. Vals AI also reports that Fable 5 attains second place with roughly 15 turns and 40 calls per task, compared with roughly 47 turns and 173 calls for GPT-5.6 Sol at a similar score. It says source relevance matters more than citation count and that longer answers are not necessarily more accurate. HLAB likewise shows task-type variation and substantial effects of the available file tools and skills on agent behaviour.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source bases its claims on benchmark scores, expert-authored legal tasks, LLM grading, and agent cost, latency and tool-use traces—not observed changes in employment or legal-service delivery.
pts.d: Legal Research Bench contains 413 lawyer-authored, peer-reviewed questions: 5 public samples, 200 private validation questions and 208 private test questions. Published results use only the test set. Rubrics contain 1–31 mandatory items, averaging 9.35. GPT 5.4 grades responses; Vals AI reports 87.4% agreement with a three-expert majority versus 83.4% average agreement for an individual human reviewer with that majority. This is judge-validation evidence, not a human-versus-AI legal-work productivity comparison. For HLAB, Vals AI independently runs Harvey's held-out benchmark using Harvey's generation and grading protocol; GPT 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge submissions, with final scores averaging their task pass rates. HLAB is Harvey's benchmark, not Vals AI's Legal Research Bench or Harvey's BigLaw Bench. The aggregate index averages benchmark scores within finance, coding and legal, then weights those sectors using GDP shares of approximately 8.0%, 5.6% and 1.2%, respectively, normalised over 14.8%. Vals AI expressly calls this weighting an oversimplified proxy. The document supplies benchmark evidence for capability and deployment tradeoffs, but no measured client outcomes, net labour savings or market displacement.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern the supplied 2026 live-leaderboard snapshot and its specified agent environments; no deadline for autonomous legal practice or workforce substitution is stated.
pts.d: The document dates Index v2 to August 13, 2026, when Legal Research Bench and HLAB were added to the returning legal sector. The earlier CaseLaw component had been removed on May 4, 2026 because Vals AI considered it saturated. Consequently, the reported rankings and claims of rapid progress are snapshot- and benchmark-version-dependent, rather than a fixed longitudinal measure. Legal Research Bench evaluates US federal and state legal research with a shared five-tool harness, internet research and a three-hour limit per task. HLAB evaluates file-based legal work with six tools, DOCX/PPTX/XLSX skills and internet access disabled. Strict completion scores require every criterion to pass; partial-credit scores answer a different question. HLAB's Fable 5 result includes fallback to Opus 4.8 on four tasks: Vals AI reports 11.25% with fallback and 10.42% if those tasks count as failures. Vals AI also reports fixing DOCX tracked-change preservation for judging, without changing the scoring rubric. These conditions qualify the scope of the capability claims; the source does not establish a date when outputs can safely be relied upon without human verification.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source directly addresses organisations selecting AI systems and legal professionals whose research and work-product tasks are being benchmarked, especially junior associates and paralegals.
pts.d: Vals AI explicitly links Legal Research Bench to research routinely performed by junior associates and paralegals: finding statutes and cases, applying precedent and synthesising across jurisdictions or regulatory regimes. HLAB broadens the relevant workflow to file-based legal work across practice types, including corporate M&A, finance, intellectual property, privacy, real estate and private-client work. Organisations making deployment decisions are offered model-specific accuracy, cost and latency comparisons; the cross-sector index also addresses finance and coding users. Clients and users of legal answers are indirectly implicated by the source's warning that plausible but incomplete answers may omit critical points, but no client-harm study is presented. The source does not distinguish consequences by law-firm size, quantify displacement of junior staff, or make claims about ALSP market share, pricing changes or access to justice.
